cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: The haloed Christ stands silent in the centre while a seated judge in a tall hat points at him from his throne and a man at the right gestures mockingly. The verse above reads 'they opened their mouth wide against me, and said, Aha, aha, our eye hath seen it'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:monumental-castelseprio-nativity.summary: The Virgin reclines on a mattress in the landscape, while the swaddled Christ Child lies in a manger above with the ox and ass; at the right an angel announces the birth to the shepherds, and below the midwives prepare the bath. The airy, sketchy brushwork gives the familiar scene unusual freshness.
facts: The frescoes of Santa Maria foris portas were rediscovered under later plaster only in 1944; their date and the origin of their painter remain controversial, though the first half of the 9th century is increasingly favoured.
They show strong Byzantine influence combined with a freedom of handling recalling late antique painting, and are often described as the finest early medieval pictorial cycle in Italy.

cur:objects-berlin-metz-christ-doctors-c.summary: Three horizontal registers tell three Gospel stories: at the top the boy Jesus sits among the teachers in the Temple, in the middle Christ changes water into wine at the wedding at Cana, and at the bottom he heals a leper. The many small figures move with a lively, rhythmic energy characteristic of Carolingian ivory carving at Metz. Read together, the scenes show Christ revealing his wisdom and his divine power at the beginning of his public life.
facts: Metz, the see of Charlemagne's son Drogo, was one of the leading centres of Carolingian ivory carving in the 9th century.
Plaques arranged in narrative registers like this one were usually set into book covers (type).

cur:objects-bm-nativity-adoration-magi-i.summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a throne holding the Christ Child on her lap, while the three Magi in Persian caps approach from either side bearing gifts and an angel stands behind. In a band beneath, the Nativity is shown with the Child in the manger. The solemn, hieratic arrangement presents the Child as King, receiving the homage of the nations.
facts: Commons classifies the panel as a 6th-century Byzantine ivory displayed in Room 41 of the British Museum.
Showing the Magi approaching a frontally enthroned Virgin and Child, rather than in profile, was an Eastern innovation of the 6th century (type).

vam:O111822.summary: A youthful, beardless Christ with thick dark hair looks out from a field of gold tesserae in this fragment of wall mosaic. It has been identified as the head of Christ from the apse of San Michele in Africisco at Ravenna, a church dedicated in 545 when the city had been won back for Justinian's empire. Much of what is visible — the gold ground, the blue tunic and red mantle, the right eye and the nose — is crude 19th-century restoration, but the hair, the flesh of the face and the left eye are original late-antique work.
facts: John Charles Robinson bought the head in Italy in 1856 as a 'fragment of an ancient wall mosaic. Roman'; it was long thought to be a 5th-century head of a saint from Sant'Ambrogio in Milan, until in 1988 it was identified as coming from San Michele in Africisco.

The apse mosaics of San Michele were sold in 1842 to an agent of King Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia; after damage in Venice and repeated restorations they went to Berlin, where the main apse mosaic survives today.
The V&A records that the gold-glass background is no older than the 19th century, added by restorers working for dealers to make the fragment look complete.
vam:O111822.notes: Heavily restored; the V&A identifies the original parts as the hair, the flesh of the face and the left eye. Bibliography: I. Andreescu-Treadgold, 1990; Buckton (ed.), Byzantium, 1994, cat. 73.
